concepts.label: Primitive Key-Value Operations (upsert/insert/replace/get/remove)
concepts.reused_or_minted: reused - Python's upsert(docid, document)/insert/replace/get/remove pseudo-code block describes the exact same operation set as the promoted sdk:kv-operations ('the SDK's direct document get/insert/upsert/replace/remove API, as opposed to queries'), confirming cross-SDK stability of this id.

notable_absence.finding: The promoted registry models data:document as 'a subset of data:item, not a synonym' but this Python page never uses the word 'item' at all, and defines a document purely in its own terms ('an entry in the database'). Nothing on this page asserts or denies the item/document distinction, so no isSubtypeOf relation is added from this page's evidence - it would have to come from a page that actually states it.

cross_component_finding: The page explicitly frames primary-key SQL++ lookups (SELECT ... USE KEYS / WHERE META(...).id = ...) as an alternative access path to the same primitive KV operations, 'though it is recommended to use the key-value API if the ID is known' - the same server-side document, reached through two different Couchbase surfaces (Query service vs Data service), exactly the kind of cross-service equivalence the registry already tracks elsewhere via mayDelegateOperationTo/hasEquivalentEffectAs.
cross_product_finding: Direct confirmation of cross-SDK vocabulary reuse: Python's upsert/insert/replace/get/remove primitive set matches sdk:kv-operations' Java-derived definition operation-for-operation, and the counters section matches Java's extraction-layer sdk:atomic-counters and sdk:document-expiration ids closely enough to justify reuse rather than minting Python-specific duplicates - both mechanisms (increment/decrement atomicity constraints under XDCR, and 'most operations implicitly remove existing expiration') are stated in near-identical language to what the Java-derived labels describe. The one operation-naming difference worth flagging: Python exposes counters through `collection.binary().increment()/.decrement()` (a `Binary.Collection` sub-object) rather than the generic `get()`/`upsert()` pair the page's own 'Use Cases' section says the *newer* high-level abstraction wraps them in - so Python's docs describe TWO counter surfaces (legacy binary incr/decr, and get/upsert-based) on one page, whereas the registry's Java-derived label ('Atomic Counters (binary increment/decrement)') only names the first. Not a rejection of reuse, but the id's label is narrower than what Python's page actually documents.
